tracks.label: Opening
tracks.text: Chapter 4. Field Identification. In April 1934, a 25-year-old art teacher at a school near Boston published a slim book that several publishers had already turned down. His publisher, Houghton Mifflin, printed just 2,000 copies and paid him no royalties on the first thousand. The printing sold out within weeks. The teacher was Roger Tory Peterson, and the book was A Field Guide to the Birds. Its idea was simple, and Peterson made it work better than anyone before him: you do not need a bird in your hand to name it. You need to know the few visible marks that separate it from every similar bird, and where and when it lives. More than ninety years later, field guides and identification apps still build on that idea. This chapter teaches you the method behind it, one step at a time. This chapter turns the anatomy of the first three chapters into a practical skill: naming the bird in front of you. You will learn the order in which experienced birders gather evidence. First comes size and shape, which usually tells you the family (the level of classification Chapter 1 told you to learn first). Then come field marks, read with the standard names for the parts of a bird, which build on the feather groups of Chapter 1. Then come behavior, habitat, range and season, where the wing shapes and flight styles of Chapter 2 and the bills of Chapter 3 earn their keep. The last section shows how field guides are organized and how to keep a checklist, the record you will submit in Chapter 8. Identifying birds by ear waits for Chapter 5.

tracks.label: 4.1 Size and shape first
tracks.text: Section 4 point 1. Size and shape first. Most beginners look at a new bird’s color first. Experienced birders start somewhere else. The Cornell Lab of Ornithology teaches four keys to identification, in this order: size and shape, color pattern, behavior, and habitat. Size and shape come first for good reasons. You can judge them in poor light, against the sky, or at a distance where color disappears, and they change far less than plumage does with sex, age and season. Shape also usually tells you the bird’s family, and as Chapter 1 showed, knowing the family narrows thousands of possible species to a handful. The Cornell Lab’s own example makes the point: an Evening Grosbeak (Coccothraustes vespertinus) and an American Goldfinch (Spinus tristis) are both yellow, black and white, but the grosbeak is far larger and has a much thicker bill. Size is harder to judge than it sounds, because a bird alone in a tree or in the sky has nothing to compare it with. The cure is a set of reference birds you know well. Three common North American species make a good yardstick. A House Sparrow (Passer domesticus) is 15–17 cm long, a little shorter than a new pencil. An American Robin (Turdus migratorius), the running example of this book, is 20–28 cm. An American Crow (Corvus brachyrhynchos) is 40–53 cm, nearly twice a robin’s length. A Rock Pigeon (Columba livia), at 30–36 cm, fills the gap between robin and crow. Figure 4.1 draws the first three to scale. Describe a new bird in these terms: “a bit bigger than a sparrow,” “robin-sized,” “smaller than a crow.” Field guides give a bird’s length from the tip of the bill to the tip of the tail, measured with the bird stretched out. A living bird hunches its neck and tilts its tail, so it looks shorter than its listed length. Weather changes apparent size too: a sparrow fluffed against the cold looks plumper than the same bird on a summer afternoon, because it is trapping warm air in its feathers, the insulation you met in Chapters 1 and 3. Size judged against a bird standing next to the mystery bird is reliable; size judged against your memory of a bird is not. Shape is a set of proportions, which Kenn Kaufman and other guide authors call structure. Look at the bill: its length compared with the head, and its form, whether a seed-cracking cone, a thin insect-picking tweezer, a hook or a flat duck bill (Chapter 3 explained what each does). Look at the size of the head, the length of the neck and legs, the length and tip shape of the tail (notched, square or rounded), and the wings, short and rounded or long and pointed (Chapter 2). Posture matters as well: a robin stands fairly upright on a lawn, a woodpecker clings upright to bark, braced on its stiff tail. Figure 4.2 shows six common families that can be named from outline alone. Proportions often settle cases that plumage cannot. Downy Woodpeckers (Dryobates pubescens) and Hairy Woodpeckers (Dryobates villosus) are both black and white with a white stripe down the back. The Downy is smaller, 14–17 cm against 18–26 cm, but size is hard to judge on a lone bird. The better test is the bill: the Downy’s is clearly shorter than its head, while the Hairy’s is about as long as the head. Small hawks give the same lesson. Female Sharp-shinned Hawks (Accipiter striatus) are about a third larger than males, which brings them close to the size of a male Cooper’s Hawk, so experienced observers rely on structure instead: Cooper’s Hawks have a larger head and a rounded tail tip, Sharp-shinned Hawks a smaller head and a square-tipped tail. Birders also speak of a bird’s jizz (also written GISS), the overall impression of size, shape and movement that lets an expert name a distant bird at a glance. The word is slang and its origin is uncertain, but the skill is real: it is shape and size, absorbed through practice until you no longer notice you are using them. Treat your first impression as a hypothesis to be tested, not a conclusion. The next sections show how field marks, behavior and context test it. A common misconception: Color is the first thing to look at, because that is what makes each bird different. In fact, Color changes with light, distance, sex, age, season and molt, and many unrelated birds share the same colors. Size and shape are visible in almost any light and usually tell you the family, which is why the Cornell Lab’s method starts there. Color pattern comes next, to separate species within the family.

tracks.label: 4.2 Field marks and bird topography
tracks.text: Section 4 point 2. Field marks and bird topography. A field mark is a visible feature that helps tell one species from similar ones: a stripe over the eye, bars on the wing, spots on the tail, a patch of color on the rump. Peterson built his 1934 guide around this idea. Instead of describing every feather, he showed similar species together and pointed out only the marks that separate them, an approach often described as identification by elimination, combining field marks with knowledge of range. His guides became famous for small arrows pointing straight at the marks that matter. Every modern guide, from Sibley’s paintings to photographic guides, still works this way. To use field marks you need words for where they are. Birders and ornithologists share a standard vocabulary for the outside of a bird, called bird topography (Figure 4.3). On the head, the crown is the top, the forehead is in front of it and the nape is the back of the neck. The lores are the small area between the eye and the bill. A stripe above the eye is the supercilium, or eyebrow; a ring of feathers around the eye is an eye-ring. A dark stripe running back from the base of the lower bill, between the cheek and the throat, is a malar stripe. The bill has an upper and a lower mandible. The body divides into upperparts and underparts. Above are the back, the rump just in front of the tail, and the tail itself. Below are the throat, breast, belly, the flanks along the sides under the folded wing, and the undertail coverts, the feathers that cover the base of the tail from below. On a perched bird the folded wing shows rows of covert feathers overlapping like roof shingles. When the coverts of two rows have pale tips, they form two pale lines across the wing, the wing bars. Behind them lie the tertials, the innermost flight feathers, and at the wingtip the primaries, the remiges you met in Chapter 1. Now read a familiar bird with these words. An adult American Robin has a blackish-gray head with white arcs above and below the eye, a broken eye-ring rather than a complete one. The bill is yellow. The throat is white with dark streaks, the breast warm orange, and the lower belly and undertail coverts white. The back and wings are gray-brown, with no wing bars. Females are usually paler than males, but the two overlap. Each item in that description names a part, so anyone with a field guide can check it. Field marks matter most when two species look alike, and the best marks are often about pattern and where color sits rather than the exact shade. Male House Finches (Haemorhous mexicanus) have red mostly on the head, breast and rump, with brown streaks on the flanks. Male Purple Finches (Haemorhous purpureus) look as if they were dipped in raspberry juice: the pinkish-red washes over the back and wings too, and the flanks lack distinct streaks. Females are easier still. A female Purple Finch has a bold face pattern, with a whitish stripe over the eye, a dark brown cheek and a dark stripe down the side of the throat; a female House Finch has a plain brown face. Field marks vary, so never rely on just one. Males and females often differ, as in the finches. Young birds differ from adults; a juvenile robin has a spotted breast. Many species change plumage between breeding and nonbreeding seasons, and molt and feather wear change a bird’s appearance through the year, as Chapter 1 described. Light matters too: the same red can look orange in low sun or brown in shade. A guide shows a typical bird in good light. Your bird may differ in small ways, and the marks that separate it from its look-alikes are the ones to check. A common misconception: If a bird doesn’t look exactly like the picture in my guide, it must be a different species or a rarity. In fact, Individual birds vary with sex, age, season, molt, feather wear and light, and a guide can show only typical birds. Check the specific marks that separate the species from its look-alikes. Most birds that look a little off are ordinary birds in an unusual plumage or light.

tracks.label: 4.3 Behavior, habitat, range and season
tracks.text: Section 4 point 3. Behavior, habitat, range and season. How a bird moves is often as telling as how it looks. An American Robin on a lawn runs a few steps, stops abruptly, and often stares at the ground with its head cocked to one side before it lunges for a worm. Chapter 3 showed that it may be listening as well as looking; for identification, the rhythm itself is the mark. A White-breasted Nuthatch (Sitta carolinensis) climbs down tree trunks headfirst, which no woodpecker does; woodpeckers hitch upward, propped on their tails. An Eastern Phoebe (Sayornis phoebe) pumps its tail down and up as it perches. You can learn these habits from a distance, long before you can see a single field mark. Flight behavior connects directly to Chapter 2. A Turkey Vulture (Cathartes aura), the bird that finds carrion by smell in Chapter 3, soars with its wings raised in a shallow V, a shape called a dihedral, rarely flaps, and teeters from side to side as it rides the air. A Red-tailed Hawk (Buteo jamaicensis) soars on flat wings. On a distant bird with no visible color, the angle of the wings can be all you need. Hovering, which you studied in Chapter 2, works the same way: a bird that hangs in front of a flower on a blur of wings is almost certainly a hummingbird. Habitat is the kind of place a bird lives, and most species are faithful to theirs. The Cornell Lab’s example is the Killdeer (Charadrius vociferus), a plover that runs about on open, grassy ground, often far from water. Woodpeckers need trees, ducks need water, and marsh birds need marshes. Habitat is a guide rather than a rule, because migrants turn up in odd places when they stop to rest and feed (Chapter 7). A bird in the wrong habitat is worth a second look, not an automatic dismissal. Range and season tell you which species are possible at all. A field guide’s range map shows where each species breeds, winters and passes through. The Ruby-throated Hummingbird (Archilochus colubris) is the only hummingbird that breeds in eastern North America, so a hummingbird in an Ohio garden in July is almost certainly that species before you see a feather. Season can mislead as well as help. Many American Robins do not migrate at all. In winter they gather in roaming flocks, eat fruit and roost in trees, so they vanish from lawns; robins have been reported in January in every U.S. state except Hawaii. The “first robin of spring” is often a local bird that has switched back to defending a territory on a lawn. Put the clues together the way a detective weighs evidence. The Cornell Lab advises keeping a running mental list of the birds most likely in your place and season. Common birds are common, so a rare species needs stronger evidence than a familiar one. Three tests show that an identification is right. First, several independent lines of evidence agree: size, shape, pattern, behavior, habitat, range and season. Second, you have ruled out each look-alike with a specific mark, not just matched a picture. Third, the record can be checked by someone else, through notes, a sketch, a photograph or a recording. eBird, the online checklist program you will meet in Section 4.4, applies the same logic: reports that are unusual for the place and date are flagged and reviewed by experienced local birders before the data are used. A common misconception: All robins fly south for the winter, so the first robin you see in spring has just returned. In fact, Many American Robins stay through the winter across much of the United States. They form flocks, eat fruit and roost in trees, so they disappear from lawns. The spring robin on your lawn is often a local bird that has switched from flocking to defending a territory.

tracks.label: 4.4 Using a field guide and a checklist
tracks.text: Section 4 point 4. Using a field guide and a checklist. Peterson’s 1934 guide was small enough to carry and arranged for use outdoors. Similar species were drawn side by side in the same pose, and the text described only the marks and ranges that separate them. Its success, and the many editions that followed, helped turn bird watching from the hobby of a few naturalists into a popular pastime. Modern guides, including David Sibley’s and Kenn Kaufman’s, follow the same plan with better art, photographs, range maps and far more plumages. Most field guides arrange species in taxonomic order, the sequence of the official checklist, which keeps relatives together. North American guides usually begin with ducks and geese and end with the songbirds, the passerines of Chapter 1. This is why learning families pays off: once you know that a bird is a woodpecker or a finch, you can turn straight to that section and compare all its members on facing pages. Use the index for names, and the illustrated quick-reference pages many guides include to find a family by shape. Each species account repays a careful read. The illustrations show the plumages you are likely to meet (male and female, adult and young, breeding and nonbreeding) and often point out the key marks with labels or arrows. The text adds size, voice, habitat and behavior. The range map shows where the species breeds, winters, lives year-round and passes through on migration, usually in different colors; check each guide’s key, because the colors differ between guides. Illustrated guides show an idealized bird with every mark visible; photographic guides show real birds, in whatever light the photographer had. Apps such as the Cornell Lab’s free Merlin suggest species from a photo or a recording. Treat their suggestions the way you treat your own first impression: as a hypothesis to test with the method of this chapter. Keep field notes, and write before you look at the book. Record the date, time, place, habitat and weather, then describe the bird part by part with the vocabulary of Section 4.2, and add a rough sketch, however crude; even a few lines showing where the stripes fall on the head will help. Notes made before you open a guide record what you saw; notes made after tend to record what the picture showed. Good notes are also the evidence that lets someone else check an identification, the third test in Section 4.3. A checklist is a list of the species you identified on one outing, with numbers. eBird, launched in 2002 by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and the National Audubon Society, collects such lists from birders worldwide. Each checklist records the place, date, start time, duration, distance traveled and number of observers, and asks whether you are reporting every species you identified. A complete checklist answers yes. That matters to science: if a complete list from a marsh in May lacks a species, the species was probably not detected there, so researchers can measure absence as well as presence and correct for effort. In Chapter 8 you will submit a standardized count of your own. A common misconception: If an identification app names the bird, the identification is done. In fact, Apps give suggestions based on probability and pattern matching, and they can be wrong when a photo is blurry, a recording is noisy, or the bird is unusual. A suggestion is a hypothesis. It becomes an identification when the bird’s size, shape, field marks, behavior, range and season all agree with it and the look-alikes have been ruled out.
